title: Recap problems: loops, arrays & patterns
overview: A recap module that combines everything so far: loops over test cases, sums with a formula, factorials in `long long`, reading until a condition is met, diamonds and other patterns, and several array tasks (counting, toggling, difference from the maximum, frequency of the minimum). Each program is a short, complete solution you can re-type from memory.

concepts.explain: `while (t--) { ... }` repeats the body `t` times and handles one case per round.
1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. This takes O(1) time instead of a loop, but compute it in `long long`.
Factorials grow very fast: 13! already overflows `int`, and 20! is about 2.4×10^18, which just fits in `long long`.
`while (scanf("%d", &x) == 1)` keeps reading until input ends, and `break` stops early.
For a value that is 0 or 1, `v = 1 - v` flips it.
For an array of 0s and 1s, the sum is the number of 1s, and `n - sum` is the number of 0s.
First find the minimum or maximum, then use it in a second loop (differences, counting how often it appears).

files.title: Babul's Vowels
files.what: Prints `Vowel` if the letter is a, e, i, o or u, and `Consonant` otherwise.
steps: Compare it with the five vowels using `||`.
files.output_note: `e` is a vowel, so the output is `Vowel`.

check.q: How could a `switch` express the same check?
check.a: `case 'a': case 'e': case 'i': case 'o': case 'u':` all fall through to printing Vowel, and `default` prints Consonant.

files.title: Sum of odd numbers strictly between X and Y

problem.name: Codeforces group - S. Sum of Consecutive Odd Numbers

files.what: For each test case, swaps X and Y if needed so X is the smaller one, then adds every odd number strictly between them.
steps: Read `x, y`. If `x > y`, swap them using `tmp`.
Loop `i` from `x+1` up to `y-1`, adding `i` to `sum` when `i % 2 != 0`.
files.complexity: Time O(|X−Y|) per test · Space O(1)
files.input_note: T, then T lines of X Y.
files.output_note: The outputs are 3+5+7+9 = `24`, then 7+9+11 = `27` (the pair was given in reverse order), then `0` (4 and 5 have nothing between them).

check.a: The task does not promise X < Y. Without the swap, the loop from `x+1` to `y-1` would run zero times.

files.title: Summation from 1 to N (formula)

problem.name: Codeforces group - G. Summation from 1 to N

files.what: Uses Gauss's formula n(n+1)/2 in `long long` instead of a loop.
steps: Compute `n * (n + 1) / 2`. One of n and n+1 is always even, so the division is exact.
files.output_note: For n = 100000, the sum is `5000050000`, which is more than an `int` can hold.

check.q: Why read `n` as `long long` even if n fits in `int`?
check.a: `n * (n + 1)` is calculated in `int` when n is an `int`, and it overflows before the division.

files.title: Count zeros and ones
files.what: Counts the 1s by adding up the values; the number of 0s is whatever is left.
steps: `number_of_ones += numbers[i]`: each 1 adds one and each 0 adds nothing.
files.input_note: n, then n values that are each 0 or 1.
files.output_note: Four 1s and six 0s, so the output is `6 4`.

check.q: Why don't we need an `if` inside the loop?
check.a: The values are only 0 or 1, so adding them up counts the 1s directly.

files.title: Factorial (T test cases)
files.what: For each test, multiplies 2 × 3 × … × n into a `long long` that starts at 1.
steps: Set `fact = 1`. This already gives the right answer for n = 0 and n = 1.
Multiply by every `i` from 2 to n.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per test · Space O(1)
files.input_note: T, then T values of N (0 ≤ N ≤ 20).
files.output_note: The outputs are `120`, then `1` (0! = 1), then `2432902008176640000` (20!, the largest the task allows).

check.q: What is the first n whose factorial overflows a 32-bit `int`?

files.title: Factorial: read all, then print all
files.what: The same factorial task, but split into three phases: read every input into an array, compute every answer, then print them all.
files.output_note: The output is the same as the first version: `120`, `1`, `2432902008176640000`.

check.q: Why is a fixed size of 15 safe here?

files.title: Toggle the X-th value
files.what: Flips the value at 1-based position X (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0) and prints the array.
steps: Print the array, each value followed by a space.

check.q: Give another expression that flips a 0/1 value.

files.title: Number triangle up and down
files.what: Prints rows 1, 12, 123 … up to 12…n, then shorter rows pushed right by leading spaces.
steps: Upper part: row `i` (1..n) prints the digits 1 to i with no spaces.
Lower part: row `i` (1..n-1) prints `i` spaces, then the digits 1 to `n-i`.
Each row ends with a newline.
files.output_note: There are 7 rows. After `1234`, the rows become ` 123`, `  12`, `   1`: each has one more leading space and one digit fewer.

check.q: How many rows are printed for n = 5?

files.title: Fixed Password
files.what: Reads password attempts one by one and prints `Wrong` until the attempt is 1999. Then it prints `Correct` and stops.
files.complexity: Time O(k) for k attempts · Space O(1)
files.input_note: One attempt per line; one of them is 1999.
files.output_note: The output is `Wrong`, `Wrong`, `Correct`. The last attempt, 4321, is never read because the loop has already stopped.

check.q: What does `scanf` return when there is no more input?
check.a: `EOF` (-1), which is not 1, so the loop ends.

files.title: Salami again (difference from max)
files.what: Finds the largest amount, then prints how much each cousin is missing compared with it.
steps: While reading, keep `max` updated. It starts at -10, which works because every amount is positive.
In a second loop, print `max - salami[j]` for each cousin.
files.output_note: The maximum is 8, so the output is `3 6 0 5 4 `.

check.q: Why can finding the max and reading happen in the same loop?
check.a: Each value only needs to be compared once as it arrives, so no second pass is needed for the max.

files.title: Shape 3 (diamond with 2N rows)
files.what: Draws a diamond: the top half widens from 1 to 2N−1 stars, and the bottom half repeats those rows in reverse.
steps: Top half, row `i` (0..n-1): print `n-i-1` spaces, then `2*i+1` stars.
Bottom half, row `i` (0..n-1): print `i` spaces, then `2*(n-i)-1` stars.
`putchar` prints one character at a time, and no spaces are printed after the stars.
files.output_note: There are 6 rows with 1, 3, 5, 5, 3 and 1 stars. The widest row appears twice in the middle.

check.q: How many leading spaces does the first row have for N = 5?

files.title: Lucky Array
files.what: The array is Lucky if its minimum value appears an odd number of times.
files.output_note: The minimum is 2 and it appears 3 times. 3 is odd, so the output is `Lucky`.

files.title: Memo and Momo
files.what: Checks which of `a` and `b` are divisible by `k` and prints Both, Memo, Momo or No One.
steps: Check the 'both' case first, because it is the most specific.
Then check `a` alone, then `b` alone; otherwise print `No One`.
files.output_note: Both 12 and 18 are multiples of 6, so the output is `Both`.

check.q: Why must the 'Both' check come first?
check.a: If `a % k == 0` were checked first, a case where both divide would stop there and print only `Memo`.

files.title: Min, max and their positions
files.what: Finds the minimum and maximum values and the 0-based index of each one's first occurrence.
steps: Start with `min = max = a[0]` and both positions at 0.
For each `i`, a strictly smaller value updates `min` and `min_pos`, and a strictly bigger value updates `max` and `max_pos`.
Print `min max` on one line and `min_pos max_pos` on the next.
files.output_note: The first line is `1 9`. The second is `2 1`: the first 1 is at index 2 and the first 9 is at index 1. The later copies are ignored because of the strict comparisons.
files.watch_out: The file name suggests a 'replace min and max' task, but the program stops after finding them. To finish that task, swap `a[min_pos]` and `a[max_pos]` and print the array.

check.q: How would you swap the minimum and maximum in the array?
check.a: Use a temporary variable to exchange `a[min_pos]` and `a[max_pos]`, then print the array.

practice_links.name: S. Sum of Consecutive Odd Numbers

recap: `while (t--)` is the simplest way to loop over test cases.
Use formulas when you can (n(n+1)/2), and do the maths in `long long`.
A factorial up to 20! fits in `long long`, but 13! already overflows `int`.
Many array tasks take two passes: first find the min or max, then use it.
For patterns, write each row's leading spaces and item count as formulas.

check_yourself.q: How would you print how often each number from 1 to M appears in an array?
check_yourself.a: Use a frequency array `cnt[M+1]` filled with 0, do `cnt[a[i]]++` for every element, then print `cnt[1]` to `cnt[M]`.

check_yourself.q: How do you add up the digits of N?
What does `while (t--)` do when `t` is 0 at the start?
check_yourself.a: Nothing. The condition is 0 (false) straight away, and `t` becomes -1.

check_yourself.q: Why is n(n+1)/2 always a whole number?
check_yourself.a: Of two consecutive numbers, one is even, so the product can always be divided by 2 exactly.

body: By now your toolbox is small and complete enough to be useful: an if-else ladder, a loop, a loop inside a loop, and an array. This module adds nothing to it. The difficulty has moved somewhere else, to a question you now have to answer before typing anything: which of those four does this problem want?
That is worth practising on its own. Reading a problem takes a minute, typing the solution takes three, and almost every problem here announces itself in a single phrase.
intro.trace:
phrase in the problem      what it asks for
-----------------------    ----------------------
"T test cases follow"      read T, loop T times
"sum of 1 to N, N huge"    a formula, not a loop
"keep reading until..."    while + break
"print N rows of..."       nested loops, count
"the largest / smallest"   store it, walk twice

body: Take the last row of that table, because it is the one that catches people. Everybody got a different amount of salami; for each person, print how much less they got than the person who got the most.

Try it in one pass and you stop at once. At the moment you read the first amount you do not yet know the maximum, so there is nothing you can print. The maximum is only certain after the final value has arrived. So the values have to be kept, and the work splits into two walks over the array: the first finds the maximum, the second prints `max - a[i]`.
intro.trace:
a:        5   2   8   3   4
walk 1:   max becomes 5, 5, 8, 8, 8
          so max = 8
walk 2:  8-5 8-2 8-8 8-3 8-4
output:   3   6   0   5   4

body: **When a loop is the wrong tool.** Adding 1 + 2 + ... + N with a loop is perfectly fine for N = 1000. If N is a few billion the loop will never finish inside the one second you are given, while the school formula `n * (n + 1) / 2` produces the same answer with one multiplication. Noticing that a loop can be replaced by arithmetic is a habit worth starting today.

**When the type is the wrong tool.** 20 factorial is about 2,400,000,000,000,000,000. An `int` stops at roughly 2,100,000,000, so the answer quietly turns into nonsense long before you reach 20. `long long` holds it. Whenever a problem multiplies many numbers together, estimate how large the answer can get before you choose the type.

**The two-walk shape again, in disguise.** "Is the number of times the smallest value appears odd?" is the same problem wearing different clothes: walk once to find the smallest, walk again to count the boxes holding it, then let `count % 2` decide the answer. Counting zeros and ones is shorter still, because adding the values up counts the ones for you, and the zeros are `n` minus that.

**Reading when you are not told how much.** Some problems never say how many lines follow. `while (scanf("%d", &x) == 1)` keeps going as long as a value arrives, and `break` leaves the moment the value you were waiting for turns up.

Three traps run through the whole day. Positions are counted from 1 in the statements but from 0 in the array, so "toggle the X-th value" means the box `a[x-1]`. Patterns here need spaces in front of the rows, so count the spaces as carefully as you count the stars. And the output words are exact: `Lucky` is not `lucky`.
The programs below are deliberately short. Read each problem first, decide out loud which of the shapes above it is, and only then check yourself against the code.
